title: Third commandment (CCC 2168–2195)
hook: Sunday rest, worship and time for family and the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second commandment: God's name held with love, and every person's name as sacred. Your line was names are holy. Whose name did you learn? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

Sunday, 9:14 p.m. An email lands with the subject line: quick question. It isn't quick, and it isn't really a question. The laptop opens, and the evening is gone. Somewhere else, a family has had pancakes, gone to Mass, visited an aunt in a nursing home, and is now arguing cheerfully over a board game. Both are Sundays. Only one of them looks like a different day from the other six. This is the commandment that sets a day apart.
screen: `SUNDAY, 9:14 P.M.` → `QUICK QUESTION.` → `A DAY THAT LOOKS DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: In Exodus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day." The Catechism roots it in creation: God worked six days, and on the seventh he rested. Rest, then, isn't laziness. It's something God himself is pictured doing. In Jewish tradition, the Sabbath is the seventh day, and the Catechism honors it as a sign of the covenant and a day of freedom: even servants and animals rest. Jesus keeps the Sabbath, and in Mark, in the Douay-Rheims, he says: "Therefore the Son of man is Lord of the sabbath also." Christians came to gather on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection, and called it the Lord's Day. The Catechism quotes Justin Martyr, an early Christian writer, on believers gathering on the day of the sun, and in the same passage Justin describes people from town and country coming together on the day called Sunday to hear the apostles' writings and to share the Eucharist. So the Catholic Sunday has two sides. Worship: Catholics are obliged to take part in Mass on Sundays and holy days, unless excused for a serious reason like illness or the care of infants. And rest: the Catechism asks Catholics to avoid work or business that gets in the way of worship, joy, works of mercy and the relaxation of mind and body. Then it widens the circle. Sunday, it says, is time for family, too often scattered during the week. Time for the sick, the infirm, the elderly. Time for reflection, silence and study. And it adds a line for employers, and for anyone whose Sunday leans on someone else's work: don't make needless demands that keep others from keeping the Lord's Day. Rest, in this commandment, isn't only for you. It's for the neighbor who would otherwise be working your Sunday.
screen: `GOD RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `LORD OF THE SABBATH ALSO.` · `THE LORD'S DAY: MASS AND REST.` · `TIME FOR FAMILY AND THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest this Sunday. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead to the coming Sunday. Choose one thing you'll set down: the inbox, the errand that can wait, the scroll. Then choose one thing to put in its place: a meal that isn't rushed, a walk, a visit to someone who's alone. If you go to Mass, picture walking in without hurry. If you pray, you can offer the day to God now, in advance. If you don't, just let the plan sit for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Third commandment. Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day: for Catholics, Sunday, the Lord's Day, kept with Mass, rest, family, and care for the poor and sick. Today's word.
Your line: keep holy the day. Today, write down the one thing you'll set aside this Sunday, and the one thing you'll do instead. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday, or a Saturday evening vigil Mass, by going to Mass and resting from unneeded work; families may set aside the day for a shared meal, visits and time together.

myth: Catholics may never work at all on Sunday
the Catechism allows for family needs and important service; what it asks is to avoid work that gets in the way of worship and rest.
the Catechism says Sunday is time for the sick and the elderly
it names family, the sick, the infirm and the elderly, and works of mercy.

the Catechism asks people not to make needless demands that keep others from keeping the day.

fork.setup: it's Sunday, and you run a small shop. you could ask your one employee to come in for a few extra hours of sorting stock that could easily wait. what does the Catechism ask?
options: call her in; work is work.
avoid needless demands that keep others from the Lord's Day.
fork.reveal: the Catechism asks Christians not to make needless demands that would keep others from keeping Sunday.

original.note: Hebrew: Sabbath, the day of rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: go to church on Sunday.
what it means: Mass and rest on the Lord's Day, with time for family, the sick, the poor and silence.
what a scholar hears: the seventh-day rest of creation, Mark 2:28, and Justin Martyr's 'day called Sunday'.

notes: CCC 2168–2195 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Mass obligation and excuses (illness, care of infants) follow CCC 2181; rest and needless demands follow CCC 2184–2187; family, sick, elderly follow CCC 2186.
Justin Martyr's date deliberately left out under the claims rule; 'an early Christian writer' used instead.
Jewish Sabbath described only as the CCC frames it (sign of the covenant, rest for servants and animals); please check the description is fair and not a foil.
Exodus 20:8 and Mark 2:28 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording.
howItsDone mentions the Saturday evening vigil Mass (CCC 2180 cites canon 1248 on anticipated Mass); confirm.
Editor: varied the hook's closing formula (several days in a row ended 'Today's commandment...'); practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.

Editor pass 2: Mark 2:27 was the large screen line of day 1119 three days earlier, so the teach now quotes Mark 2:28 (CCC 2173 cites 2:27–28), with screen, match, trapdoor and sources aligned; 'Christians, from the early Church' softened to 'came to gather'; the Justin Martyr sentence now separates what CCC 2174 quotes (the day of the sun) from what the same chapter of the Apology describes (town and country, the apostles' writings), which CCC 1345 quotes.

Audit (y4 1122–1131): 'employers and shoppers' softened; CCC 2187 names employers and 'every Christian', not shoppers. Exodus 20:8, Mark 2:28, the Justin Martyr split and the CCC 2181–2187 paraphrases checked and found sound.
